title: Search strategy and operators
note: Search tools match words, not ideas. Split your question into two or three main concepts, list synonyms for each, join synonyms with OR inside parentheses, and join different concepts with AND. Quotation marks keep a phrase together; truncation catches word endings.

read.title: Building a search string
text: Suppose your question is whether exercise improves sleep in older adults. A database does not understand that sentence; it matches words. So first pull out the main concepts: exercise, sleep, older adults. Leave out filler words like "whether" and "improves" that authors may not use.

Next, list synonyms for each concept, because authors describe the same idea in different ways. Exercise might appear as physical activity or training; older adults as elderly or aged. Join the synonyms for one concept with OR and wrap them in parentheses. Then join the concepts with AND:
(exercise OR "physical activity") AND sleep AND ("older adults" OR elderly OR aged)

OR widens each concept, and AND requires every concept to be present, so the results are both broad and on target. Quotation marks keep phrases together, and a truncation symbol such as sleep* would also catch sleeping and sleepiness.

Then judge the results. If you get thousands of loosely related records, add a concept or use filters such as date or study type. If you get only a few, add synonyms or broaden a term. Keep a short log of each search so you can repeat it and report it later.

q.q: Why are words like "whether" and "improves" left out of the search?
o: Authors may not use them, so they can block relevant records
They make the search too broad

q.q: In the search string, what does AND do?
o: Requires every concept to be present

q.q: What does the reading suggest when a search returns only a few results?
o: Switch to a stricter date filter
Add synonyms or broaden a term
